tr.td: 26 to 29 July 1950, in the first weeks of the Korean War
A double railroad underpass near the hamlet of No Gun Ri, Yongdong County, North Chungchong Province, South Korea
United States aircraft and soldiers of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Cavalry Division
South Korean refugees, mostly women, children and older people; the number killed is disputed

li.a: Military.com: The No Gun Ri Massacre: When American Soldiers Killed Hundreds of South Korean Refugees
Encyclopedia.com: Survivors of the No Gun Ri Incident (the 1997 survivors' petition)
Milwaukee Independent: Forgotten Victims: How panic and paranoia led to a massacre of refugees at the No Gun Ri Bridge
CNN: Clinton expresses regret over No Gun Ri deaths of Korean civilians, January 11, 2001
PBS NewsHour: Joint No Gun Ri Report Released
Asia Times: Belated American apology for Korean War massacre

content.p: For three days at the end of July 1950, South Korean villagers who had been told to leave their homes were trapped beneath a railroad bridge while American troops fired into its two tunnels. The dead were mostly women, children and older people. The killing began with an air attack on a column of refugees on the tracks and went on with rifle and machine gun fire from the ridge above. It took place a month into the Korean War, near a hamlet called No Gun Ri, about 100 miles southeast of Seoul.

The survivors tried for decades to be heard. Under South Korea's authoritarian governments they feared reprisals if they spoke, and nearly all their petitions were ignored. The story reached a wide international audience only in September 1999, when the Associated Press published its own investigation. In January 2001 the United States Army acknowledged that its soldiers had killed an unknown number of refugees there, but called the event a tragedy inherent to war and not a deliberate killing. South Korean investigators disagreed. No American has been punished, and the survivors turned down the memorial and scholarship fund the United States offered in place of compensation.

North Korean forces crossed into the South on 25 June 1950 and caught the arriving American troops unprepared. Task Force Smith, the first American unit to meet the invaders, was overrun on 5 July. On 20 July Major General William Dean, who commanded the 24th Infantry Division, was captured at Taejon. Asia Times describes the first American soldiers as men fresh from garrison duty in occupied Japan, physically untrained and mentally unprepared for combat in Korea.

The 7th Cavalry Regiment, the unit once led by Custer, landed at Pohang-dong on 18 July as part of the 1st Cavalry Division. According to Military.com, half its sergeants had just been moved to other units and many of its soldiers were teenagers who had never been in combat. The Army's later report described the soldiers involved as "young, undertrained, under-equipped and new to combat", under officers with little combat experience, according to PBS.

They arrived in a country in flight. Military.com puts the number of South Koreans fleeing south in those first weeks at an estimated 380,000, and says intelligence reports warned that enemy soldiers were slipping through American lines disguised as refugees. Asia Times writes that fear of guerrillas in civilian clothes had spread through the American units.

The extent to which commanders had ordered troops to fire on refugees became the central argument of the case. Military.com lists several documents from those days. On 24 July a message logged at the 8th Cavalry Regiment's headquarters said refugees were not to cross the front line and that anyone who tried should be fired on, adding the phrase "use discretion in case of women and children". Major General William Kean, commanding the 25th Infantry Division, ordered that "all civilians seen in this area are to be considered as enemy and action taken accordingly." Major General Hobart Gay, whose 1st Cavalry Division included the 7th Cavalry, said to journalists that he took most civilians heading for American positions to be North Korean guerrillas, and he later described refugees as "fair game". On 4 August, after the No Gun Ri killings, Gay ordered the bridge at Waegwan over the Naktong River blown up while hundreds of fleeing Koreans were still crossing it, Military.com says.

PBS reported that a CBS News report had cited a military memo dated the day before the No Gun Ri killings. It said the Army was worried that "large groups of civilians, either composed of or controlled by North Korean soldiers, are infiltrating U.S. positions" and instructed warplanes to fire on groups of refugees heading toward American lines. Asia Times, describing orders displayed at the site today, says that on 25 July aircraft were ordered to strafe civilians approaching American lines and that on 26 July civilians in the combat zone were to be treated as hostile.

The people who died came mainly from the village of Chu Gok Ri and the hamlets around it. According to the survivors' own account, set out in a petition they sent to President Clinton in 1997, two American soldiers and a Korean policeman came to the village around noon on 23 July and told everyone to leave because a battle was about to be fought there. Most villagers walked about two kilometres to a mountain hamlet, Im Ke Ri, where they thought they would be safe.

On the evening of 25 July American soldiers arrived at Im Ke Ri, gathered the villagers and promised to escort them to a safe place toward the city of Pusan. The column that set off numbered 500 to 600 people on foot, some leading ox carts piled with belongings and some carrying children on their backs. They spent that night in a stream bed at Ha Ga Ri. According to the petition, the soldiers had gone by dawn, and the refugees walked on by themselves along the main route south.

Around midday on 26 July they reached the railroad crossing at No Gun Ri, where a few American soldiers stopped them. Survivors say the soldiers made everyone stand on the tracks and searched their belongings. Military.com reports that the search turned up no weapons and no sign that any of them were guerrillas. The petition adds a further claim, that the soldiers radioed for a machine gun and bomb attack and then left. Whatever was said on the radio, the soldiers left, and aircraft appeared soon afterwards.

The planes strafed the crowd on the embankment. Some survivors estimated, according to Military.com, that roughly 100 people died there before anyone reached cover. Gunfire from American positions then drove the survivors into a larger double tunnel beneath a concrete bridge, each barrel about 80 feet long, 22 feet wide and 40 feet high, according to Military.com.

The 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry had dug in on a ridge above. Military.com says the unit was in poor shape: on the night of 25 July its men had panicked and scattered during a disorganised retreat from positions near Yongdong, and more than 100 were missing until the battalion was regrouped the next morning. Larry Levine and James Crume, who handled communications, recalled afterwards that the order to open fire on the refugees came down from above, probably from division headquarters. A mortar round landed among the refugees, Military.com says, followed by what Levine called a "frenzy" of small-arms fire. Norman Tinkler, a machine gunner in H Company, said he fired about 1,000 rounds into the tunnels and had seen "a lot of women and children" on the tracks. Joseph Jackman, who served in G Company, recalled for the BBC his commander running down the line and shouting at the men to shoot. Herman Patterson, a former rifleman, said of the mindset: "It was assumed there were enemy in these people."

Inside, the survivors piled the dead into barriers against the bullets. Some tried to dig into the ground with their hands. Thirst drove them to a small stream that ran through the underpass, its water mixed with blood. "Children were screaming in fear and adults were praying for their lives, and the whole time they never stopped shooting," Park Sun-yong, who lost a four-year-old son and a two-year-old daughter, said. Another survivor, Park Hee-Sook, told the AP: "I didn't want to die, so I piled the dead bodies on top of me." The petition says anyone who stepped out was shot, and that medics who came by a couple of times only watched.

By the second day, Military.com says, the firing had thinned into scattered shots and occasional bursts whenever someone moved. Not every American took part. First Lieutenant Robert Carroll, a reconnaissance officer with H Company, said he stopped some of the shooting and carried a wounded child back to a surgeon. The regiment pulled out in the early hours of 29 July. That afternoon North Korean soldiers reached the tunnels and, according to Military.com, allegedly fed the survivors, roughly two dozen and mostly children, and sent them back toward their villages.

The toll has never been settled, and each figure comes from a different party. Two North Korean journalists who arrived with the advancing troops reported about 400 bodies in the area, 200 of them in one tunnel, Military.com says. The survivors also put it at around 400. The AP's 1999 report gave an estimated 300 to 400 killed, according to the Milwaukee Independent. On the day of the joint report, PBS wrote that South Korean investigators believed up to 250 died, while the American report said no more than 100 and possibly as few as 50. CNN gave the range as 100 to 300.

In 2005 South Korean officials certified the names of 163 people dead or missing and 55 wounded, and noted that many other victims had never been reported, Military.com reports. The No Gun Ri Peace Foundation has estimated 250 to 300 dead, mostly women and children. Asia Times writes that civilians had also been killed in American air attacks in the days before, which is part of why it says no fully agreed figure exists, and it gives a range of 163 to 300.

Under the authoritarian rule of President Syngman Rhee, survivors feared retaliation for talking, and Yang Hae-chan, who was ten in 1950, says police warned him to keep quiet. Asia Times says the postwar governments in Seoul kept the subject taboo because disclosure of American atrocities could have damaged the alliance with Washington, and that a novel about No Gun Ri was banned in 1977. It also says a high-ranking American officer told a US reporter in September 1950 that a US regiment had killed many civilians, but nothing came of it.

Chung Eun-yong, a former policeman, lost his two young children in the tunnels; his wife, Park Sun-yong, survived badly wounded. Military.com says he filed his first petition in 1960 and that he and a committee of survivors went on to submit more than 30, nearly all ignored. He spent three decades collecting evidence in archives in Seoul and Daejeon. In 1994, after South Korea's return to democracy, he published a novel based on the events after ten publishers turned it down. The Army's position was that any killing of civilians had happened in the heat of combat. Asia Times says the book set off a wave of coverage in 1994, and that July that year survivors travelled to the United States to give testimony, including at the Pentagon.

In September 1997 Chung sent a petition to President Clinton, asking for recognition of the killings, a formal apology and compensation. It was rejected, according to Encyclopedia.com. The turning point came when the Associated Press took up the case. Military.com says the reporters Sang-Hun Choe, Charles J. Hanley and Martha Mendoza got in touch with Chung in 1999, whereas the Milwaukee Independent dates his handing over of evidence to 1998. They interviewed survivors and American veterans and found declassified documents on orders to shoot civilians. Encyclopedia.com says the team went through hundreds of boxes of military records at the National Archives and tracked down more than 100 veterans. It also says the reporters rebuilt the movements of the battalion to show it had been at No Gun Ri when the Army had denied it. The AP published on 29 September 1999. Encyclopedia.com quotes the AP as reporting that six 1st Cavalry Division veterans said they themselves shot into the crowd of refugees, and that six others said they saw the killing.

The AP report did not go unchallenged. PBS notes that U.S. News and World Report questioned the accuracy of one of the AP's main sources, a veteran named Edward Daily. When the AP went back to him in May with new information, he accepted that he could not have been at the shooting and must have been repeating what he heard second-hand. Reporter Martha Mendoza told PBS that Daily's account of a large number of civilians being shot in South Korea was nevertheless true, and said that, as she understood it, the Pentagon had told the New York Times it had concluded that more than 100 people died.

Military.com adds that Carroll later said his part in the story had been twisted. He said that no orders to fire were given, that no machine guns fired, and that only about a dozen refugees were wounded, mostly by shrapnel. Patterson said that when he described a massacre, he meant what happened to his own unit in combat and not the refugees. An Army historian, Major Robert L. Bateman, wrote a book contesting the AP's claims, arguing that poor training, poor leadership and unreadiness at a time when troops were told to crack down on refugees explain the shooting, and that no order to fire on civilians was given.

After the AP story the Pentagon and the South Korean government ran parallel inquiries. Defense Secretary William Cohen said investigators had spoken to nearly 150 Americans and reviewed more than 1,000 documents. Both governments released their conclusions on 11 January 2001, after about 15 months, PBS reports.

The American report was the first formal acknowledgment of US military involvement in the killing of Korean refugees in July 1950. According to Military.com, it said American soldiers had killed "an unknown number" of South Korean refugees with "small-arms fire, artillery and mortar fire, and strafing", but called it "an unfortunate tragedy inherent to war and not a deliberate killing" and said it had found no evidence of an order to shoot. The South Korean report said 17 veterans of the 7th Cavalry testified that they believed such orders existed, two of them battalion communications specialists well placed to know. The record that might have decided the question, the regiment's July 1950 communications journal, was missing from the National Archives, and Military.com says no one could explain why.

Some of the Pentagon's own outside advisers disagreed with the result. Military.com reports that former congressman Pete McCloskey, a Marine veteran of the Korean War and one of eight advisers, agreed with the Koreans. Retired Marine General Bernard Trainor wrote to Cohen that the American command "failed to control the fire of its subordinate units and personnel" at the very least and "ordered the firing" at worst. Chung Eun-yong said: "This is not enough for the massacre of over 60 hours, of 400 innocent people who were hunted like animals", the same page says.

President Clinton's statement the same day said: "On behalf of the United States of America, I deeply regret that Korean civilians lost their lives at No Gun Ri in late July 1950." He said the two governments had been unable to determine precisely what happened but had concluded that innocent Korean refugees were killed or injured. PBS noted that he did not apologise and did not mention the role of American troops. He promised a memorial to the victims and "all other innocent Korean civilians killed during the war" and a commemorative scholarship fund. Asia Times puts the proposed payment at $4 million, shaped as a memorial and scholarship fund and covering all American killings of civilians in the war, which it says may number as many as 200 incidents. The survivors' association declined the money. A journalist at the Hankyoreh newspaper told a 2020 forum that refusing it protected the claims of victims in other cases.

Later disclosures sharpened the dispute. Military.com reports that the AP found at least 14 declassified documents in the inquiry's own archived files in which senior commanders ordered or authorised shooting refugees, including the "fair game" remarks and an instruction to "shoot all refugees coming across river". Military.com says the Army's published report, which ran to 300 pages, contained none of them. In 2005 the historian Sahr Conway-Lanz found a letter from US Ambassador John Muccio to the State Department dated 26 July 1950. It said that, at a high-level meeting, a policy had been decided to shoot refugees approaching American lines after warning shots. The Pentagon acknowledged it had seen the letter in 2000 and dismissed it, saying it described a "proposed policy". The letter itself, Military.com notes, referred to "decisions made".

South Korea's National Assembly passed a law in 2004 to set up a committee to identify victims, which produced the 2005 certification. The 33-acre peace park at No Gun Ri opened in 2011 with a memorial, museum and education centre, built with $17 million from the South Korean government. Bullet scars remain in the concrete of the tunnels. Chung Eun-yong died in August 2014, aged 91, and his son Chung Koo-do now chairs the foundation. Military.com says the AP's reporting encouraged survivors of other killings to come forward, which led to South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission investigating further cases.

In November 2020 an American retiree, Jorja Elliott-Reyburn, whose father went missing in the early days of the war, visited the site to apologise in person. Survivors received her without anger, Asia Times reported. The same article notes that no official American compensation has been paid and that no prosecution has been aimed at the officers or men involved. Military.com reaches the same conclusion, that no American soldier was ever punished, and says some veterans still deny the massacre while others say it happened but was not ordered.
